criteria.criterion: Run cargo test: a test loads athena.toml (planning for hard jobs only), and shows a reading marked hard runs the planner and critic while an ordinary reading runs neither.
criteria.evidence: The test with_athena_toml_planning_hard_jobs_only_a_hard_reading_runs_the_planner_and_critic_and_an_ordinary_one_does_not reads the [job_plan] table from athena.toml with include_str and asserts enabled plus mode Hard. A reading with hard_reason set runs reader, planner, critic, producer, verifier and writes job-plan-1.json and critique-1.json. A null hard_reason runs only reader, producer, verifier and writes neither file. A companion test checks that mode=all plans both readings and enabled=false plans neither. I ran it and both tests passed. The new test cannot pass without the run/mod.rs change, because the old gate planned whenever enabled was true.

criteria.criterion: Run cargo test: a test shows athena status reports, separately for planned and unplanned landings, how many were later cited as the cause of a failure, revert or fix job, beside the landed share.
criteria.evidence: The CLI test lands one planned (hard) job and one unplanned job. It then asks for a fix citing the planned job, a revert citing the unplanned one, and a plain 'document' request. It asserts the status text lines 'planned   1 of 1 landings cited (0 failure · 0 revert · 1 fix) · 1 of 1 jobs landed (100%)' and the matching unplanned line, plus the JSON keep_rule.later_harm fields. The core unit test covers failure introspections and excludes the job's own introspections, earlier ones, and requests that only cite a job. Both passed.

criteria.criterion: athena.toml [job_plan] is set so planning runs for hard jobs only (git diff shows the change), and crates/athena-data/src/config.rs parses and validates the setting.
criteria.evidence: athena.toml changes enabled=false to enabled=true and adds mode="hard". config.rs adds a PlanMode enum (All is the default, Hard), deserialized in lowercase, so an unknown value fails to parse; the test an_unknown_plan_mode_is_refused checks this. It also adds JobPlanConfig::plans(hard), where enabled=false wins over any mode, with tests. The repo-config test asserts plans(true) and !plans(false). The athena-data tests passed.

findings.summary: Three changed files are not on the expected deliverables list
findings.evidence: display.rs renders the new status lines, which criterion 2 needs. outputs.rs holds the reader's hard_reason schema text, where the hardness definition (criterion 5) lives; the reading expected that definition in reading.rs, and it is close to, but is not, a prompt file. hestia.rs changes a test fixture to switch planning off, because athena.toml now turns it on. Each change is small and needed, but none is on the list.

findings.summary: The later-harm counts show only when at least one planned job exists
findings.evidence: later_harm is a field of KeepRule, and keep_rule() returns None when no job is planned. With planning off, or before the first hard job, status shows no unplanned later-harm counts either. With mode="hard" now on, planned jobs will appear, so the effect is limited.

findings.summary: Revert and fix causes are found by matching words in free request text
findings.evidence: has_word looks for revert/fix word forms in a later request that also names the job id as a whole token. The docs and D143 say this is a floor, not a census, and the verdict does not use it. Still, it is coarse: a request such as 'don't revert X, fix Y' that names a landed id would count. No dedicated revert record kind exists, so the reading's assumption of 'revert records' was met from request text instead.

summary: The change passes: it does what the request asks. athena.toml now sets [job_plan] enabled = true, mode = "hard". config.rs parses that mode, rejects unknown values, and keeps enabled = false as a full off switch. The run plans a job only when its reading carries hard_reason, the same marking that already escalates the producer. The reader's schema now defines a hard job as the request does: a rule that can refuse or hold work, landing, the history check, records, the run pipeline or the drain. athena status shows, under the keep rule, a planned line and an unplanned line: how many landings were later cited in a failure introspection, a revert request or a fix request, next to that group's landed share. The same counts are in --json. I ran the targeted tests and all passed: hard versus ordinary planning with the repository's own athena.toml, the other modes, config parsing, the hardness schema text, and the status counts end to end through the CLI. fmt, clippy and the full test suite (1526 tests) passed in Athena's recorded checks. job-planning.md section 9, the new D143 decision and the CHANGELOG all record the change and why, citing job 20261027-054211-a2n5. There are three minor findings: three small, needed edits fall outside the deliverables list; the counts are hidden until at least one planned job exists; and revert and fix causes are found by word matching, which the docs say only gives a floor.
